Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: The threat items are oriented toward external environmental danger (scanning surroundings, planning escape routes), which is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 68-year-old policy analyst unless there is an additional trauma context not represented here.

Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance reinforces an expectation of unpredictable external danger, which fits assault/combat-type trauma more than illness trauma and does not cohere well with the rest of the illness-based profile.

Memory: Guilt on Recall and Negative Appraisals: Character Blame imply a strong self-blame/guilt formulation, but the other selected items center on current danger vigilance and emotional loss; for life-threatening illness, this specific self-blame pattern is possible but, combined with the external-danger threat items, creates a clinically incoherent mix of trauma themes.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, persistent escape-route scanning is hard to reconcile with the trauma context. It implies imminent external attack or entrapment rather than illness-related threat, while the rest of the profile centers on bodily danger and emotional change.

Intense guilt on recall is not impossible after severe illness, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals focus on permanent emotional loss and bodily alarm rather than responsibility for causing harm or failing others. The guilt theme lacks support elsewhere in memory or appraisals.

'The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am' suggests a strong characterological self-blame formulation. In a life-threatening illness case, that can occur, but in this profile it is not well integrated with the other selected appraisals, which focus on bodily danger and emotional numbing. Together with guilt on recall, it introduces a self-blame theme that is otherwise unsupported.

vignette: Malcolm sat at the edge of his desk when the pain arrived, a sudden, crushing weight that dropped him onto the polished floor of his office. Paramedics found him unresponsive and rushed him to the intensive care unit, where they intubated him and administered paralytics to keep his lungs moving while his heart stuttered through dangerous arrhythmias. For four days, Malcolm remained conscious but completely immobilized, watching the clinical staff adjust his settings while machines regulated his breathing. He understood he was dying, and the terror of being locked inside a failing body, unable to command his own chest, left a permanent imprint. When the sedation finally lifted and he was moved to a step-down ward, the immediate panic subsided, but the physical aftermath did not. The tension settled into his shoulders and jaw, never fully releasing. Malcolm found himself checking the deadbolts on his front door and the windows in his study long after they were secured, certain that if he stopped monitoring the perimeter, he would be caught off guard. His body remained constantly tense, braced as if expecting another sudden collapse. At work, the difficulty concentrating made his role untenable. He sat before stacks of legislative drafts and budget projections, but his eyes would slide across the text without taking hold. He would reread the same paragraph repeatedly, losing the thread of the argument, his attention fracturing whenever a colleague's pen clicked in a steady rhythm. The sound pulled him back to the ICU ventilator's metronome pace; he would have to stop his work, press his palms flat against the desk, and wait until his breathing settled. He began leaving the policy analysis wing an hour early, telling his supervisor he was managing fatigue, though the truth was that the fluorescent lights and the hum of office equipment felt like a countdown to another crisis. The memories of the hospital did not arrive as quiet reflections. Sometimes they slid over him with a chilling flatness; he could describe the sterile air, the taste of the breathing tube, the weight of the paralytic, but he felt completely numb, as if recalling a stranger's nightmare. Other times, the past refused to stay in the past. He would be unlocking his car and suddenly the ground beneath him felt like the hospital mattress, the blanket pressing down, his lungs burning for air he could not draw. He had to stop mid-stride, gripping the door handle until his knuckles turned white, until the present rushed back. When the emotion finally broke through, it was overwhelming; he would sit in his living room, hands shaking, and force himself to close his eyes and breathe, knowing that pushing through only left him hollow. He had come to believe he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, that the quiet satisfaction of a finished report or the comfort of a morning coffee belonged to a man who no longer existed. What frightened him most was his own physiology. He watched his pulse in the morning light, counting beats, measuring breaths, certain that his body kept reacting as if he were still in the ICU long after he was safe. He could no longer trust his own body to keep him upright, to regulate his breathing, to simply carry him through a day without warning of another failure. Over the months, the avoidance habits hardened into routine. Malcolm stopped chairing the annual policy review, delegating his sections to junior analysts and citing vague health appointments. He avoided gyms, then grocery stores, then the community center where his late wife had volunteered, because crowded spaces made his chest tighten and his shoulders knot. He began scheduling every errand for early Tuesday mornings, when the parking lots were empty and the roads quiet. Now, at sixty-eight, he sat in the waiting room of a community mental health clinic, his hands folded tightly over his knees. He had come because his daughter finally insisted he stop managing alone, because the silence in his house had grown too heavy, and because he could no longer ignore the way his days were shrinking. He hoped someone might help him quiet the constant scan of the room, might help him understand why his own chest felt like a locked space, and might help him remember how to live without waiting for the next alarm.
